en: To make worse; to impair.

ex.en: The economy steadily worsened.
ex.ja: 景気は着実に悪くなった。

note.ja: worse（より悪い）+ -en。「悪化する」。

en: The act or state of declining or sinking.
The measure or beat of movement.
To give a cadence to.
To give structure to.

cadence.ety: Borrowed from Middle French cadence, from Old Italian cadenza (“conclusion of a phrase of music”), from Latin *cadentia (literally “a falling”), form of cadēns, the present participle of cadō (“to fall, to cease”). The Latin verb is inherited, via Proto-Italic *kadō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱad-e- (“to fall”, thematic present). Doublet of cadenza and chance.

note.ja: ラテン語 cadere（落ちる）から。声の調子が「下がる」こと →「抑揚・終止形」。cadet、accident と同じ cad。

en: A method of transforming a text in order to conceal its meaning.
A cryptographic system using an algorithm that converts letters or sequences of bits into ciphertext.
To write in code or cipher.
Of an organ pipe: to sound independent of the organ.

cipher.ety: 14th century. From Middle English cifre, from Old French cyfre, cyffre (French chiffre), ultimately from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty”), from صَفَرَ (ṣafara, “to be empty”). Doublet of chiffre and zero. Sense 8 (a fault in an organ valve) may be a different word.

note.ja: アラビア語 ṣifr（ゼロ・空）から。「ゼロ」→「暗号」→「取るに足らない人」。zero と同じ語源。

en: A woodwind musical instrument that has a distinctive liquid tone whose characteristics vary among its three registers: chalumeau (low), c…

clarinet.ety:
Borrowed from Italian clarinetto, diminutive of clarino (“trumpet”) (as the first clarinets had a strident tone similar to that of a trumpet), from Latin clarus.
Alternatively, the word may come from French clarinette, diminutive form of clarine (“bell”), from clarin, from clair (“clear”), from Latin clarus.

ex.en: Neither Tom nor Mary can play the clarinet.
ex.ja: トムとメアリーは二人ともクラリネットを吹けない。

ex.en: Neither Tom nor Mary plays the clarinet.
ex.ja: トムとメアリーは両方ともクラリネットを吹かない。

ex.en: Neither Tom nor Mary knows how to play the clarinet.
ex.ja: トムとメアリーは二人ともクラリネットの吹き方を知らない。

note.ja: フランス語 clarinette から。clarine（鐘）、ラテン語 clarus（明るい・はっきりした）。clear と同じ。

en: The act or process of condensing or of being condensed.
The state of being condensed.

condensation.ety: From condense + -ation, borrowed from Latin condēnsātiō, condēnsātiōnem.

note.ja: condense（凝縮する）+ -ation。con + densus（濃い）。「結露・凝縮」。dense と同じ。

ex.en: They live on the 12th floor of this condo.
ex.ja: 彼らはマンションの１２階に住んでいる。

note.ja: condominium の短縮。con（共に）+ dominium（所有）。

en: The act of combining that occurs where two rivers meet.
The place where two rivers, streams, or other continuously flowing bodies of water meet and become one, especially where a tributary join…
To join together into one stream.

confluence.ety: From late Middle English confluence, from Late Latin cōnfluentia (“a flowing together, conflux”), from cōnfluēns (present participle of cōnfluō (“to flow or run together”)) + -ia (nominal suffix).

note.ja: con（共に）+ fluere（流れる）。「合流（点）」。influence、fluid と同じ flu。

en: A state of the bowels in which the evacuations are infrequent and difficult, or the intestines become filled with hardened faeces.
The act of crowding anything into a lesser space, or the state of being crowded or pressed together; condensation.

constipation.ety: First attested in the beginning of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English constipacioun, borrowed from Medieval Latin constīpātiō or its Old French equivalent, from cōnstīpō + -tiō. By surface analysis, constipate + -ion.

ex.en: I'm suffering from chronic constipation.
ex.ja: 慢性的な便秘で苦しんでいます。

note.ja: ラテン語 constipare（詰め込む）から。con + stipare（押し込む）。「便秘」。

en: That gives advice or consultation; advisory.

consultative.ety: From Latin-type *cōnsultātīvus (probably used in Medieval Latin), from cōnsultāt-, past participial stem of cōnsultō, + -īvus. By surface analysis, consult + -ative.

note.ja: consult（相談する）+ -ative。

en: Any goods which are illicit or illegal to possess.

Prohibited from being traded.

contraband.ety: From Spanish contrabanda (modern spelling contrabando), from Italian contrabando (modern spelling contrabbando), from contra (“against”) + bando (“ban”), and reinforced by French contrebande.

note.ja: イタリア語 contrabbando から。contra（反して）+ bando（布告）。「布告に反する品」→「密輸品」。

en: The art and practice of preparing food for consumption, especially by the application of heat; cooking.

cookery.ety: From Middle English cokerie, kokery, equivalent to cook + -ery.

note.ja: cook（料理する）+ -ery。「料理法」。

en: A device to assist in motion as a cane, especially one that provides support under the arm to reduce weight on a leg.
Something or someone that supports, often used negatively to indicate that it is not needed and causes an unhealthy dependency; a prop.
To support on crutches; to prop up.
To move on crutches.

crutch.ety:
From Middle English crucche, from Old English cryċċ (“crutch, staff”), from Proto-West Germanic *krukkju, from Proto-Germanic *krukjō (“crutch, staff”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewg- (“wrinkle, bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend”).
Cognate with Scots curche, crutch (“crutch, stilts”), Dutch kruk (“crutch”), Low German krukke, Krück (“crutch”), German Krücke (“crutch”), Swedish krycka (“crutch”). Latin crucia, crucca, croccia, crocia (“crutch”), and its descendants are ultimately from the Germanic.

ex.en: I broke my leg and am on crutches.
ex.ja: 足を折ってしまって、松葉杖なの。

ex.en: I broke my leg and am walking on crutches.
ex.ja: 足を骨折して、松葉杖ついてるんだ。

ex.en: A young girl on crutches asked Tom where he lived.
ex.ja: 松葉づえの若い女性はトムに住んでいるところを聞いた。

An administrator.

custodian.ety: From a shortening of Latin custōdiānātus, from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”). By surface analysis, custody + -ian.

ex.en: The policeman was shot in the leg by a delinquent.

democratically.ety: Partly from democratical + -ly (suffix forming adverbs), and from democratic + -ally (variant of -ly), modelled after Middle French democratiquement (modern French démocratiquement).

ex.ja: 我々は民主的にその会議を運営した。

acting or including an agent to eliminate, reduce, mask, or control odor.

deodorant.ety: From Latin de- + odorans, present participle of odorare (“to smell”), from odor (“a smell”); see odor. By surface analysis, de- + odor + -ant.

ex.en: You should use a deodorant.

note.ja: de（取り去る）+ odor（におい）+ -ant。「消臭剤」。

en: To explode, blow up
To combust or decompose supersonically via shock compression.

detonate.ety: First attested in 1729; either borrowed from French détoner or directly from Latin dētonātus, perfect passive participle of dētonō (“to thunder down (strongly); (figuratively, of a person) to thunder, speak threateningly, to rage; to stop thundering”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- (“off, from”) + tonō (“to thunder”)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂-. The current interlingual meaning seems to be a new formation in postclassical times (to thunder → make a large noise → explode), compare explode.

ex.en: We're going to detonate the bomb in a few moments.
ex.ja: 我々はまもなく爆弾を爆発させます。

ex.en: The objective of Minesweeper is to clear the minefield without detonating the mines.
ex.ja: マインスイーパの目的は地雷原から地雷を取り除くことである。

note.ja: ラテン語 detonare（雷のように鳴る）から。de + tonare（雷が鳴る）。「爆発させる」。thunder と同系。

en: A room containing a number of beds (and often some other furniture and/or utilities) for sleeping, often applied to student and backpacke…
A building or part of a building which houses students, soldiers, monks etc. who sleep there and use communal further facilities.

dormitory.ety: From Middle English dormitory, dormytory, dormytorye, borrowed from Latin dormītōrium (“a sleeping-room”), from dormiō (“to sleep”). Doublet of dormitorium and dorter.

ex.en: Those two boys share the same dormitory room.
ex.ja: あの二人の少年は寮の同じ部屋を共有している。

ex.en: I live in the same dormitory as Tom does.
ex.ja: 僕はトムと同じ寮に住んでるんだ。

ex.en: You'll soon get used to living in a dormitory.
ex.ja: すぐに君は寮で生活するのになじみますよ。

note.ja: ラテン語 dormitorium（寝室）から。dormire（眠る）。「寮」。dormant（休眠中の）と同じ。

en: To leave the country in which one lives, especially one's native country, in order to reside elsewhere.

emigrate.ety: From Latin emigratus, perfect passive participle of emigro (“to move away, remove, depart from a place”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + migro (“to move, remove, depart”).

ex.en: They are going to emigrate to America.
ex.ja: 彼らはアメリカに移住するつもりです。

ex.en: His family emigrated from their mother country to Brazil forty years ago.
ex.ja: 彼の家族は４０年前に母国からブラジルへ移住しました。

note.ja: e（外へ）+ migrare（移る）。「（外国へ）移住する」。immigrate（入ってくる）の対。migrate と同じ。

en: The act of plucking up by the roots; an uprooting or rooting out; extirpation; utter destruction.
The state of being plucked up by the roots.

eradication.ety: Borrowed from Latin ērādīcātiō, from ērādīcō + -tiō, from ē- (“out”) + rādīx (“root”) + -ō. Equivalent to eradicate + -ion or e- (“without”) + radication.

note.ja: eradicate（根絶する）+ -ion。e（外へ）+ radix（根）。「根こそぎ取り除くこと」。radical、radish と同じ。

catlike (resembling a cat); sleek, graceful, inscrutable, sensual, and/or cunning.

femininity.ety: From Middle English femynynytee, femyninytee, variants of femynyte (archaic modern English feminity), equivalent to feminine + -ity.

ex.ja: 「女らしさ」って何？そんな言葉、私の辞書にないし。

note.ja: feminine（女性の）+ -ity。ラテン語 femina（女性）。「女らしさ」。female と同系。

Changeable.
To deceive, flatter.

fickle.ety: From Middle English fikil, fikel, from Old English ficol (“fickle, cunning, tricky, deceitful”), equivalent to fike + -le. More at fike.

note.ja: figure（形・図形）+ -ative。ラテン語 figura（形）。「形にたとえた」→「比喩的な」。

en: Fodder for animals, especially cattle and horses.
An act or instance of foraging.
To search for and gather food for animals, particularly cattle and horses.
To rampage through, gathering and destroying as one goes.

forage.ety:
From Middle English forage, from Old French fourage, forage, a derivative of fuerre (“fodder, straw”), from Frankish *fōdar (“fodder, sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder, feed, sheath”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, to feed”).
Cognate with Old High German fuotar (German Futter (“fodder, feed”)), Old English fōdor, fōþer (“food, fodder, covering, case, basket”), Dutch voeder (“forage, food, feed”), Danish foder (“fodder, feed”), Icelandic fóðr (“fodder, sheath”). More at fodder, food.
Unrelated to modern French forage (“drilling”), whose first element is ul

ex.ja: ほら、今日は海の幸だったから明日は山の幸とかさ、取りに行こうよっ。

note.ja: 古フランス語 fourrage（まぐさ）から。fuerre（飼料）、fodder と同系。「食料を探し回る」。

en: To seize something and hold it firmly.
To wrestle or tussle.
A close hand-to-hand struggle.

grapple.ety:
From Middle English *grapplen (“to seize, lay hold of”), from Old English *græpplian (“to seize”) (compare Old English ġegræppian (“to seize”)), from Proto-Germanic *graipilōną, *grabbalōną (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to take, seize, rake”), equivalent to grab + -le.
Cognate with Dutch grabbelen (“to grope, scramble, scrabble”), German grabbeln (“to rummage, grope about”) and grapsen, grapschen (“to seize, grasp, grabble”). Influenced in some senses by grapple (“tool with claws or hooks”, noun) (see below). See further at grasp.

ex.en: He grappled with his brother.
ex.ja: 彼は兄と取っ組み合った。

ex.en: The Esperanto movement has always had to grapple with the problem of 'eternal beginners'.
ex.ja: エスペラント運動は常に永遠の初心者の問題を抱えています。

note.ja: 古フランス語 grappil（引っかけ鉤）から。「鉤で引っかける」→「取っ組み合う」→ 問題に「取り組む」。grab と同系。

en: A low, mournful sound uttered in pain or grief.
A low, guttural sound uttered in frustration, disapproval, or ecstasy.
To make a groan.
To seemingly creak under the strain of being heavily laden.

groan.ety:
From Middle English gronen, granen, from Old English grānian (“to groan; lament; murmur”), from Proto-West Germanic *grainōn, from Proto-Germanic *grainōną (“to howl; weep”), from Proto-Germanic *grīnaną (“to whine; howl; whimper”).
Cognate with Scots grain (“to cry, scream”), Dutch grijnen, grienen (“to cry; sob; blubber”), German Low German grienen (“to whimper; mewl”), German greinen (“to whine; whimper”), Swedish grina (“to howl; weep; laugh”).
The noun is from Middle English gron, grone, from the verb.

ex.en: We could hear the groans of the injured man.
ex.ja: 怪我をした人のうめき声が聞こえてきた。

ex.en: The old chair groaned under her weight.
ex.ja: 彼女の体重でその椅子は、きしんだ。

ex.en: The table was groaning with food.
ex.ja: テーブルがきしむほど食物がたくさんあった。

note.ja: 古英語 grānian から。擬音的な語。「うめく」。

en: An insect, especially a beetle, at an immature stage of its life cycle.
To scavenge or in some way scrounge, typically for food.
To dig; to dig up by the roots; to root out by digging; often followed by up.

grub.ety:
From Middle English grubben, grobben, from Old English *grubbian, from Proto-West Germanic *grubb-, from Proto-Germanic *grubb- (compare Middle Dutch grobben (“to scrape, scramble, grab”), Old High German grubilōn (“to dig, search”), German grübeln (“to meditate, ponder”)), from Proto-Germanic *grub- (“to dig”) (see *grabaną).
The noun sense of "larva" is from Middle English grub, grubbe, grobbe, crubbe and may derive from the notion of "digging insect" from the verb above, or from the uncertainly related Middle English grub (“dwarfish fellow”). Compare West Frisian krobbe (“beetle”). The slan

en: To raise; to lift; to elevate (especially, to raise or lift to a desired elevation, by means of tackle or pulley, said of a sail, a flag,…
To lift a trophy or similar prize into the air in celebration of a victory.
Any member of certain classes of devices that hoist things.
The act of hoisting; a lift.

hoist.ety:
Alteration of earlier hoise (“to hoist”), apparently based on the past tense forms, from Middle Dutch hisen (“to hoist”). Compare modern Dutch hijsen (“to hoist”), German hissen (“to hoist”), Danish hejse (“to hoist”). Compare also French hisser (“to hoist”), Galician isar (“to hoist”), Spanish izar (“to hoist”), Catalan hissar (“to hoist”), Italian issare (“to hoist”),
Portuguese içar (“to hoist”), Sicilian jisari (“to hoist”), all borrowed from a Germanic source.

ex.en: Hoist your sail when the wind is fair.

ex.en: Give me a hoist.

An attractive man, especially one who is muscular.

hunk.ety: Probably borrowed from West Flemish hunke (“hunk; chunk”), of obscure origin. The sense of an attractive man is recorded in Australian slang in 1941, in jive talk in 1945.

To shovel muck from.
To manure with muck.

muck.ety: From Middle English mok, muk, from Old Norse myki, mykr (“dung”) or less likely Old English *moc, *moce (in hlōsmoc (“pigsty dung”) and lustmoce (“lady's smock (Cardamine pratensis)”)) (compare Icelandic mykja and Danish møg ("dung")), from Proto-Germanic *mukį̄ (“dung; manure”), from Proto-Germanic *muk-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mewg-, *mewk- (“slick, slippery”) (compare Welsh mign (“swamp”), Latin mūcus (“snot”), mucere (“to be moldy or musty”), Latvian mukls (“swampy”), Albanian myk (“mould”), Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “mucus, lamp wick”), Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs, “mushroom”), Germa

note.ja: 中英語 muk から。北欧語 myki（糞）。「泥・汚物」。

en: Hard to see through, as a fog or mist.
Dark, dim, gloomy.

murky.ety: From Middle English mirky. Related to Old Norse myrkr, Russian мрак (mrak) and its Slavic cognates. By surface analysis, murk + -y.

ex.en: The water in the lake is murky.
ex.ja: 湖の水は濁っている。

ex.en: His English has a murky, muddled sound to it, don't you think?
ex.ja: 彼の英語の発音って、なんかにごってない？

note.ja: murk（暗さ）+ -y。北欧語 myrkr（暗い）。「濁った・うさんくさい」。

en: Of or pertaining to the period of time immediately following birth, or to the newborn.

To make (a territory, etc.) politically neutral.

neutralize.ety: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ize.

note.ja: neutral（中性の）+ -ize。「中和する・無力化する」。

en: Something which portends or is perceived to portend either a good or evil event or circumstance in the future, or which causes a forebodi…
A thing of prophetic significance.
To be an omen of.
To divine or predict from omens.

ex.en: You're my good omen.
ex.ja: お守りはあなたよ。

ex.en: I always thought that suffering a heart attack was an omen of death.
ex.ja: 私はいつも思っていた、心筋梗塞を患うことは死期を知らせる前兆だと。

ex.en: The cap cloud above Mt. Fuji is said to be a good omen.
ex.ja: 富士山にかかる笠雲は縁起がいいと言われています。

note.ja: ラテン語 omen（前兆）から。「前兆」。abomination（不吉なものとして避ける）と同じ。

To load or stack (goods) onto pallets.

pallet.ety: From Middle English paillet, from Anglo-Norman paillete (“bundle of straw”), from Old French paille (“straw, chaff”), from Latin palea (“chaff”).
